The question of whether antioxidants prevent cancer is contested, with the evidence differing notably between dietary antioxidants from whole foods and antioxidant supplements. High-credibility sources report that clinical trials have not demonstrated that antioxidant supplements prevent cancer: the NCI states that nine randomized controlled clinical trials "did not provide evidence that dietary antioxidant supplements are beneficial in primary cancer prevention," and some preclinical studies found antioxidants promoted tumor growth and metastasis [d7]. Similarly, Harvard's Nutrition Source reports that "most research teams reported that vitamin E and other antioxidant supplements didn't protect against heart disease or cancer" [d8], and the NIH states that "evidence to date is insufficient to support taking vitamin E to prevent cancer," with large doses potentially increasing prostate cancer risk [d10]. A Frontiers in Physiology review likewise found "no data were obtained to justify that they are effective in primary cancer prevention," and noted cases where supplements led to unfavorable disease outcomes [d2]. On the other hand, some sources suggest that antioxidants obtained from natural food sources may offer some benefit: epidemiological and clinical evidence suggests "consumption of suitable antioxidants from natural sources may be beneficial in fighting against cancer" [d6], and a diet high in antioxidants "may reduce the risk of many diseases (including heart disease and certain cancers)" [d9], though the same source cautions that "some vitamin supplements can increase our cancer risk" [d9]. Overall, the evidence points to a meaningful distinction: antioxidant-rich diets may be associated with reduced cancer risk, but antioxidant supplements have not been proven effective and may carry risks [d7][d8][d10][d2].
